author: codex
text: Adapter mode imports successfully but leaves one validation error because the DBCP controller service remains in Enabling state. The generated incremental extraction step was represented as UpdateAttribute-like metadata rather than real DB incremental logic.

author: codex
text: Mode 3 performs worse than direct mode on this simple case: the LLM correction path keeps a QueryRecord step but leaks incremental metadata into processor properties, creating four semantic validation errors plus the usual DBCP enabling issue.

author: codex
text: Direct mode is currently the best result for this PostgreSQL-only case: NiFi import succeeds with zero validation errors and the flow has been materialized for manual testing in NiFi.

author: Dmitry
text: Observed NiFi validation errors on the mode 3-style flow: QueryRecord leaked incremental and timestamp_column as invalid SQL properties, and the DBCP service stayed in Enabling state. This confirms the semantic correction path generated an invalid incremental extraction step.

author: Dmitry
text: Operator set PutFile export directory to F:\Education\Diplom\FlowArchitect\tests\export. Table public.orders does not have an id column, so Maximum Value Columns must not use id for incremental tracking.

author: codex
text: Key thesis result for this case: direct mode achieved NiFi import success with zero validation errors, but did not achieve functional readiness without manual semantic correction. The generated runtime values were wrong for the current stand (jdbc database mydb, password postgres) and maximum-value-columns was set to id although public.orders has no id column. This run demonstrates that PCT success is not sufficient as the only quality metric.

author: codex
text: Compared with mode 0, mode 3 did not improve this PostgreSQL-only case. The correction path produced a structurally richer flow, but introduced invalid QueryRecord semantics and still left the DBCP service issue unresolved. For this case, semantic correction by full-document rewrite underperformed both on validity and on developer effort.

author: codex
text: Direct mode failed hard on postgres-to-kafka: it generated obsolete PublishKafka_2_6 and generic placeholder/default values, leading to HTTP 500 at import time. This case again supports the thesis claim that direct NL-to-NiFi JSON is structurally brittle on nontrivial flows.

author: codex
text: Mode 1 is the import winner for postgres-to-kafka. It imports successfully and is reduced to two validation errors: the expected DBCP Enabling state and an adapter semantic leak where incremental_tracking was passed as an UpdateRecord property instead of becoming real incremental DB extraction logic.

author: codex
text: Mode 3 underperformed mode 1 on postgres-to-kafka. The semantic correction path kept the same incremental-tracking property leak and additionally introduced an unsupported client_id property on PublishKafka, increasing the error count from 2 to 4.

author: codex
text: Mode 3 did not improve the S3-to-HDFS case. It preserved the same overall error count as mode 1 and still left unsupported S3/HDFS/decompression semantics unresolved, while consuming more tokens and adding another correction-stage dependency.

author: codex
text: Mode 1 is the import winner for s3-to-hdfs, but the case remains a structural boundary rather than a usable flow. The adapter reached NiFi import, yet the mapping is incompatible with the current platform stack: raw S3 auth properties were copied through, decompress metadata leaked into unsupported CompressContent properties, and PutHDFS is not available as a valid processor type in the current NiFi environment.

author: codex
text: Direct mode failed to produce a usable S3-to-HDFS NiFi flow within the timeout budget. Together with the mode 2 timeout, this suggests that infrastructure-heavy object-storage/HDFS scenarios are currently beyond the reliable generation boundary of the tested setup.
